steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper CiPR, a framework for generalized category discovery that uses cross-instance positive relations. Explain the GCD setting, the limitations of the baseline method, our approach, and our main contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- From closed-set recognition to generalized category discovery
  - large-scale annotated training -> superb performance
  - assumption: recognize only the same set of classes seen in training with annotations
  - limits open-world use: unannotated data, unseen categories
  - more realistic settings: semi-supervised learning (SSL), few-shot learning, open-set recognition (OSR)
  - novel category discovery (NCD): partition unlabelled data from unseen categories by transferring knowledge from seen ones
  - early NCD assumes unlabelled images all from unseen categories
  - generalized category discovery (GCD): unlabelled from both seen and unseen; Fig. 1
- The baseline GCD method and its limitations
  - we draw inspiration from the GCD baseline
  - baseline: vision transformer; supervised contrastive learning on labelled + self-supervised contrastive on all data
  - label assignment via semi-supervised k -means
  - category number estimation: examine possible numbers in a given range
  - limitation 1: labelled/unlabelled handled independently, stronger signal for labelled may compromise unlabelled representation
  - limitation 2: needs known category number for label assignment
  - limitation 3: number estimation slow, reruns clustering many times
- Our approach: CiPR and selective neighbor clustering (SNC)
  - no known unseen category number needed; Cross-instance Positive Relations (CiPR) in unlabelled data for representation learning
  - core: semi-supervised hierarchical clustering = selective neighbor clustering (SNC), inspired by parameter-free FINCH
  - specific neighbor selection for labeled vs unlabeled examples -> higher quality pseudo labels
  - SNC: reliable pseudo labels + estimate unseen category number without repeated runs
  - graph of selected neighbor relations constrained by labelled instances; clusters = connected components
  - iterative hierarchy of partitions, different granularity, respecting labelled constraints
  - one-to-one merging -> fast class number estimate; significantly faster than baseline
  - prior pseudo-positive works only use nearest neighbors; ours uses full label information, purer pseudo labels
- Contributions
  - (1) CiPR framework: cross-instance positive relations in partially labelled set, strengthens connections among all instances
  - (2) SNC: semi-supervised hierarchical clustering for pseudo labels in training and label assignment in testing
  - (3) class number estimation with SNC: intrinsic + extrinsic clustering quality, joint reference score on labelled and unlabelled data
  - (4) evaluation on generic and fine-grained datasets; state-of-the-art across the board

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Existing machine learning models can achieve superb performance when they are trained on large-scale datasets with human annotations. But the success of these models relies heavily on the assumption that they only need to recognize images from the same set of classes, with large-scale human annotations, that they were trained on. This limits how they can be used in the real open world, where we will run into data without annotations and from unseen categories. Indeed, more and more effort has gone into dealing with more realistic settings. For example, semi-supervised learning (SSL) trains a robust model using both labelled and unlabelled data from the same set of classes; few-shot learning tries to learn models that generalize to new classes with few annotated samples; open-set recognition (OSR) learns to tell whether an unlabelled image belongs to one of the classes the model is trained on or not. More recently the problem of novel category discovery (NCD) was introduced, where models learn to automatically partition unlabelled data from unseen categories by transferring knowledge from seen categories. Early NCD methods assume that the unlabelled images all come from unseen categories only. NCD was recently extended to a more generalized setting called generalized category discovery (GCD), which relaxes this assumption to reflect the real world better, i.e., the unlabelled images come from both seen and unseen categories. Fig. 1 shows an illustration of the GCD problem.

In this paper we tackle the GCD problem, taking inspiration from the baseline method. In that baseline, a vision transformer model was first trained for representation learning, using supervised contrastive learning on the labelled data and self-supervised contrastive learning on both labelled and unlabelled data. Then, with the learned representation, semi-supervised k -means was used to assign labels across all instances. Also, based on semi-supervised k -means, the baseline introduced an algorithm for estimating the unknown category number of the unlabelled data, by examining possible category numbers in a given range. However, this approach has several limitations. First, during representation learning their method treats labelled and unlabelled data independently, and the labelled data gets a stronger training signal, which might compromise the representation of the unlabelled data. Second, their method needs a known category number to perform label assignment. Third, their method for estimating the category number is slow, because it has to run the clustering algorithm many times to test different category numbers.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Existing machine learning models can achieve superb performance when they are trained on large-scale datasets with human annotations. But the success of these models relies heavily on the assumption that they only need to recognize images from the same set of classes, with large-scale human annotations, that they were trained on. This limits how they can be used in the real open world, where we will run into data without annotations and from unseen categories. Indeed, more and more effort has gone into dealing with more realistic settings. For example, semi-supervised learning (SSL) trains a robust model using both labelled and unlabelled data from the same set of classes; few-shot learning tries to learn models that generalize to new classes with few annotated samples; open-set recognition (OSR) learns to tell whether an unlabelled image belongs to one of the classes the model is trained on or not. More recently the problem of novel category discovery (NCD) was introduced, where models learn to automatically partition unlabelled data from unseen categories by transferring knowledge from seen categories. Early NCD methods assume that the unlabelled images all come from unseen categories only. NCD was recently extended to a more generalized setting called generalized category discovery (GCD), which relaxes this assumption to reflect the real world better, i.e., the unlabelled images come from both seen and unseen categories. Fig. 1 shows an illustration of the GCD problem.

In this paper we tackle the GCD problem, taking inspiration from the baseline method. In that baseline, a vision transformer model was first trained for representation learning, using supervised contrastive learning on the labelled data and self-supervised contrastive learning on both labelled and unlabelled data. Then, with the learned representation, semi-supervised k -means was used to assign labels across all instances. Also, based on semi-supervised k -means, the baseline introduced an algorithm for estimating the unknown category number of the unlabelled data, by examining possible category numbers in a given range. However, this approach has several limitations. First, during representation learning their method treats labelled and unlabelled data independently, and the labelled data gets a stronger training signal, which might compromise the representation of the unlabelled data. Second, their method needs a known category number to perform label assignment. Third, their method for estimating the category number is slow, because it has to run the clustering algorithm many times to test different category numbers.

To overcome these limitations, we propose a new approach for GCD that does not need a known unseen category number and that considers Cross-instance Positive Relations (CiPR) in the unlabelled data for better representation learning. The core of our approach is a new semi-supervised hierarchical clustering algorithm called selective neighbor clustering (SNC), which is inspired by the parameter-free hierarchical clustering method FINCH. We introduce specific mechanisms for selecting neighbors for labeled and unlabeled examples. Because it carefully takes into account the properties of labeled and unlabeled images, our method generates pseudo labels of higher quality, and these strengthen representation learning. SNC can generate reliable pseudo labels for cross-instance positive relations, and it can also estimate unseen category numbers without running the clustering algorithm repeatedly. SNC builds a graph that embeds all the subtly selected neighbor relations constrained by the labelled instances, and it produces clusters directly from the connected components of the graph. SNC iteratively builds a hierarchy of partitions with different granularity while satisfying the constraints from the labelled instances. With a one-to-one merging strategy, SNC can estimate a reliable class number quickly without repeated runs of the algorithm, which makes it significantly faster than the baseline. Some works in the literature do introduce pseudo positives for representation learning, but these methods only consider nearest neighbors, while our method incorporates a new semi-supervised clustering into training that fully uses label information and gives more reliable pseudo labels with higher purity.

Our main contributions are: (1) we propose a new GCD framework called CiPR, which uses cross-instance positive relations in the partially labelled set to strengthen the connections among all instances, which helps representation learning for better category discovery; (2) we introduce a semi-supervised hierarchical clustering algorithm called SNC, which allows reliable pseudo label generation during training and label assignment during testing; (3) we also use SNC for class number estimation, by exploring intrinsic and extrinsic clustering quality based on a joint reference score that considers both labelled and unlabelled data; (4) we evaluate our framework comprehensively on generic image recognition datasets and on challenging fine-grained datasets, and show state-of-the-art performance across the board.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
By training on large-scale datasets with human annotations, existing machine learning models can achieve superb performance (e.g., [1]). However, the success of these models heavily relies on the assumption that they are only tasked to recognize images from the same set of classes, with large-scale human annotations, on which they are trained. This limits their application in the real open world, where we will encounter data without annotations and from unseen categories. Indeed, more and more effort has been devoted to more realistic settings. For example, semi-supervised learning (SSL) [2] aims at training a robust model using both labelled and unlabelled data from the same set of classes; few-shot learning [3] tries to learn models that can generalize to new classes with few annotated samples; open-set recognition (OSR) [4] learns to tell whether or not an unlabelled image belongs to one of the classes the model is trained on. More recently, the problem of novel category discovery (NCD) [5] has been introduced, which learns models to automatically partition unlabelled data from unseen categories by transferring knowledge from seen categories. Early NCD methods assume that unlabelled images all come from unseen categories only. NCD has recently been extended to a more generalized setting, called generalized category discovery (GCD) [6], which relaxes this assumption to better reflect the real world, i.e., unlabelled images come from both seen and unseen categories. An illustration of the GCD problem is shown in Fig. 1.

In this paper, we tackle the GCD problem drawing inspiration from the baseline method [6]. In [6], a vision transformer model was first trained for representation learning using supervised contrastive learning on labelled data and self-supervised contrastive learning on both labelled and unlabelled data. With the learned representation, semi-supervised k -means [5] was then adopted for label assignment across all instances. In addition, based on semi-supervised k -means, [6] also introduced an algorithm to estimate the unknown category number for the unlabelled data by examining possible category numbers in a given range. However, this approach has several limitations. First, during representation learning, their method considers labelled and unlabelled data independently and uses a stronger training signal for the labelled data, which might compromise the representation of the unlabelled data. Second, their method requires a known category number to perform label assignment. Third, their category number estimation method is slow, as it needs to run the clustering algorithm multiple times to test different category numbers.

To overcome these limitations, we propose a new approach for GCD which does not require a known unseen category number and considers Cross-instance Positive Relations (CiPR) in unlabelled data for better representation learning. At the core of our approach is a novel semi-supervised hierarchical clustering algorithm, named selective neighbor clustering (SNC), inspired by the parameter-free hierarchical clustering method FINCH [7]. We introduce specific neighbor selection mechanisms for labeled and unlabeled examples. By carefully taking into account the properties of labeled and unlabeled images, our method generates higher quality pseudo labels which strengthen representation learning. SNC can not only generate reliable pseudo labels for cross-instance positive relations, but also estimate unseen category numbers without repeated runs of the clustering algorithm. SNC builds a graph embedding all subtly selected neighbor relations constrained by the labelled instances, and produces clusters directly from the connected components of the graph. It iteratively constructs a hierarchy of partitions with different granularity while satisfying the constraints imposed by the labelled instances. With a one-to-one merging strategy, SNC can quickly estimate a reliable class number without repeated runs of the algorithm, making it significantly faster than [6]. Although some works in the literature introduce pseudo positives for representation learning, such as [8,9,10], these methods only consider nearest neighbors, whereas our method incorporates a novel semi-supervised clustering into training that fully exploits label information and produces more reliable pseudo labels with higher purity.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows: (1) we propose a new GCD framework, named CiPR, that exploits cross-instance positive relations in the partially labelled set to strengthen the connections among all instances, fostering representation learning for better category discovery; (2) we introduce a semi-supervised hierarchical clustering algorithm, named SNC, that allows reliable pseudo label generation during training and label assignment during testing; (3) we further leverage SNC for class number estimation by exploring intrinsic and extrinsic clustering quality based on a joint reference score considering both labelled and unlabelled data; (4) we comprehensively evaluate our framework on both generic image recognition datasets and challenging fine-grained datasets, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across the board.
